summary: Lists requirements for a way to mark SIP messages so they get logged. Operators debugging customer problems often cannot predict which networks a call crosses, so end-to-end monitoring is hard. A marker on the message would flag it as a candidate for logging, usually during operator-controlled testing. This is a requirements document, not a protocol.

eli5.summary: When a package gets lost, it helps if the sender puts a bright sticker on it that tells every post office to write down where it went.

subtitle: Requirements for marking SIP messages to trigger logging across networks.

tldr.problem: Operators debugging SIP issues cannot predict the path signals take across multiple networks, making end-to-end monitoring impractical without a standard marking mechanism.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines requirements for a "log me" marker in SIP messages that indicates they should be logged at each network node they traverse, enabling end-to-end troubleshooting.
tldr.outcome: This is a requirements document, not a protocol specification. It guides the design of future logging solutions by defining 12 key requirements.

facts.label: Scope of logging
facts.value: All related dialogs in a session

today: RFC 8123 is an Informational document that defines requirements for a logging solution, not a protocol itself. It guides future specifications for adding logging markers to SIP, enabling operators to debug calls crossing multiple networks and administrative domains.

sections.title: The SIP Logging Challenge
sections.content:
Service providers and enterprises use SIP (Session Initiation Protocol) to set up phone calls and multimedia sessions. When customers report problems or new software is tested, operators need to debug issues by looking at the signals crossing their networks.

As networks grow and interconnect through transit providers and international borders, the signaling path becomes unpredictable. An operator at the start cannot list all the SIP entities the messages will traverse. This RFC describes requirements for a mechanism to mark messages as candidates for logging end-to-end.
sections.eli5: Phone calls cross many countries and companies. A network manager cannot predict which route a call will take. They need a way to mark calls so that every office that touches it writes down what happened.

sections.title: Key Concepts
sections.content:
The RFC defines three key concepts: a Network Boundary where messages pass between different administrators, a Trust Domain of networks that have agreed to participate in debugging, and an Intermediary as any SIP entity along the call path.

The trust domain is critical: only networks that have prior agreement should trust and process the logging marker. This prevents one operator from accidentally triggering logging in unrelated networks or exposing sensitive information.
sections.eli5: A network boundary is where control changes hands. A trust domain is a group of friends who agreed to help debug each other. An intermediary is anyone along the way.

sections.title: Requirements for the "Log Me" Marker
sections.content:
The RFC specifies that the marker must be insertable into requests and responses, must cross network boundaries, and must be removable if incorrectly inserted. It should include a test case identifier to correlate logged messages. SIP intermediaries must be able to base logging decisions solely on the marker's presence without maintaining state.

The marker must cover entire dialogs: once inserted, logging should continue through all related messages in a session until a stop event occurs. Endpoints, gateways, and back-to-back user agents must be able to insert it. The mechanism should allow intermediaries to request logging on behalf of endpoints that do not support marking.
sections.eli5: The marker must travel through networks, stay attached to related messages, and let any network office add it if the original sender did not. Logging should follow the entire call, not just one message.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The marker itself must not reveal sensitive information about users or devices. Its insertion at the endpoint must be approved by an authorized user or administrator. Activating debug mode must use a secure channel. Logged signaling is privacy-sensitive and must not be readable by unauthorized parties.

Most critically, the marker must be removed at trust domain boundaries unless the next hop network has agreed to participate in logging. This prevents inadvertent exposure of sensitive call information to networks that should not receive it.
sections.eli5: The marker must not reveal secrets. Turning on debug mode must be authorized and secure. Logs must stay private. Different network operators must agree in advance to share logging.

sections.title: Implementation Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC outlines a typical debugging workflow: an operator enables debug mode on a phone, the phone inserts the marker, each intermediary along the path logs the call if configured to do so, and logging stops after a defined time or event.

The document notes that log retrieval mechanisms are out of scope: logs might be accessed by connecting to the SIP entity, sent to a central server, stored on removable media, or retrieved via other methods. All mechanisms must follow the network administrator's authorization and privacy policies.
sections.eli5: An operator turns on debug mode, the marker goes through the networks, and offices write down what they see. Later, logs can be retrieved by different methods, but all must follow privacy rules.
